title: What Are the Keystone Habits for Success?
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Following up a post that asked readers to name the keystone habits for student success, Dave Stuart Jr. admits he does not know the answer but argues that teachers should still form and test hypotheses rather than wait for complete research. He offers four hunches. The first and most developed is argumentative thinking, which he distinguishes sharply from arguing to win: drawing on Graff and Birkenstein and on Richard Fulkerson, he defines argument proper as collaboratively getting to the bottom of things, and suggests pop-up debate as a way to build the habit. The second is an 'Act, Reflect, Tweak' loop illustrated by a student who started and repeatedly reshaped his own blog; the third is weekly goal setting and keeping as a grit experiment; and the fourth is recreational reading, with a caution that good habits can tip into addiction. He concludes that inspiration alone produces only short bursts of energy, whereas habits let students apply long-term effort in one direction.
points: Stuart argues that the best teachers give themselves freedom to act on hunches and test hypotheses that could be wrong rather than waiting for complete research.
He separates argument-to-win, which he says decays decision-making and relationships, from collaborative argument whose goal is a good decision rather than victory.
The Act, Reflect, Tweak loop, drawn from a student's blogging, is proposed as a habit that makes success hard to avoid.
Weekly goal review and recreational reading are offered as further candidate keystone habits, with honesty about their unproven status.
His closing claim is that inspiration fades while habits require no energy, making habit-building central to long-term student success.
quotes: The best teachers give themselves the freedom to form and test hypotheses that could be wrong. They have hunches that they act on.

When we enter into a political debate, for example, with our mind resolutely made up and our identity staked on our claim, we are highly unlikely to leave that debate with any kind of greater understanding or clarity. Our main takeaway will be: they are wrong; I am right. It seems we've discussed the issues, but actually we've just taken turns with target practice.

When we enter a decision with our mind already made up, the same is true: we'll leave with a “decision,” but it's unlikely that we've made the best one. We've used a biased scale to weigh out the options, ending up exactly where we wanted to. This is a huge deal if we want to lead a flourishing life and help our students do likewise.

I suspect that habits are a key part of the picture for increasing the success of our kids. Many of my kids leave class inspired by their progress and their visions for their futures, yet only those who have developed successful habits tend to do anything with that inspiration.
Inspiration is not enough in our classrooms, my colleagues. It leads to short-term bursts of energy; it facilitates joy; it's beautiful and it's part of why I love this work.
